tier_reason: No benchmark exists: the repo page and README give no timings and no OpenSSL comparison, and a WebSearch found no MB/s comparison; the only numbers anywhere are the third-party aesige PyPI page, which shows tgcrypto slower than an AES-NI IGE implementation.

corrections.caveats: No evidence that it beats OpenSSL. Lead not substantiated: no benchmark in README (checked current README and revisions 95ff73c, d6fbe3c, 5c2c7f3), commit titles, issues or source comments; a WebSearch for TgCrypto MB/s or OpenSSL comparisons found none. Its documented role (Pyrogram docs, WebSearch snippet only, readthedocs blocked) is to replace the much slower pure-Python PyAES fallback, so the realistic baseline is pyaes, not OpenSSL, and no numbers exist for that either. The source is a portable T-table AES, so beating OpenSSL's AES-NI based core on large buffers is implausible. Third-party package aesige (Apache-2.0, AES-NI / ARM Crypto Extensions, https://pypi.org/project/aesige/, read via the PyPI JSON API) reports tgcrypto at 14.8 us decrypt and 24.3 us encrypt for 1 KB versus 7.4 us and 7.7 us for aesige on x86_64, i.e. tgcrypto is 2-3.2x slower than a hardware-accelerated IGE (aesige author's own numbers, no CPU stated). Archived by the owner on 2024-12-23; README says the project is no longer maintained or supported. LGPL licence: the sidebar lists both LGPL-3.0 and GPL-3.0 texts; README says LGPLv3+.

notes: Metadata confirmed: archived 2024-12-23 (last commit a8aee64 'Update README.md'), 211 stars, LGPL-3.0 plus GPL-3.0 texts. Shortcoming: no measurement at all; only third-party data (aesige) shows it 2-3.2x slower than an AES-NI IGE; real incumbent is pure-Python pyaes. Low notability; kept at D per keep-and-document rule.

tier_reason: The only comparison is the rival tape-sha256 crate's BENCHMARKS.md (bench code benches/merkle_leaves.rs public, CPU models given for four of five x86 machines) against the Rust sha2 crate; rustc/gcc versions and Firedancer build flags are not stated, and the measurer competes with Firedancer, so not A and not an independent well-known suite.

corrections.caveats: The repo itself carries no baseline numbers: src/ballet/sha256/test_sha256.c --bench prints only Gbps 'Ethernet equiv throughput / core' for incremental, streamlined and batched modes (14 and 1472 byte payloads) with no OpenSSL or other baseline row (its only OpenSSL mention is a comment on generating a test vector). The only comparison is from the rival tape-sha256 crate (BENCHMARKS.md in https://github.com/spool-labs/sha256, the crate's real repository; the crates.io repository field https://github.com/spool-labs/tape-sha256 returns 404), against the Rust sha2 0.10.9 crate (which uses SHA-NI on x86 via runtime detection) rather than OpenSSL, with Firedancer built by the benchmark author, who competes with it, using unstated compiler version and flags. The harness hoists the prefix||leaf concatenation for Firedancer out of the timed region and checks every reference entry point against sha2 before timing. Batch hashing needs independent messages. Zen 5 CPU model not captured. Zen 3 (avx-8 only, 0.93x) shows the AVX batch path is not always faster than serial SHA-NI, and on Zen 4 the AVX-512 path is only about 1.9x.

notes: Numbers and derived ratios match BENCHMARKS.md exactly (Zen 5 12.55 vs 27.71 us; 9B14 22.51 vs 43.71; 7B13 45.87 vs 42.66; 8581C 21.82 vs 49.18; 6985P-C 16.89 vs 36.87). benchmark_url moved from the crates.io tarball to the GitHub BENCHMARKS.md (same commit 5e72f67). Shortcomings: no first-party comparison, rival-run harness, baseline is Rust sha2 not OpenSSL, slower than serial SHA-NI on Zen 3; last commit 2026-10-12, 1.5k stars, Apache-2.0 confirmed.

tier_reason: First-party BENCHMARKS.md with public bench code (benches/merkle_leaves.rs, poh_chain.rs, blob_group.rs) and CPU models for four machines, but the rustc version and RUSTFLAGS are not stated and the Zen 5 and Apple CPU models are not captured, so it falls short of A.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 1 star, 0 forks, 13 commits on GitHub (spool-labs/sha256); crates.io: 470 downloads (0.1.0 361, 0.2.1 109), versions 0.1.0 (2026-07-27) and 0.2.1 (2026-08-11)
corrections.claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md summary vs sha2 0.10.9: AMD Zen 5 3.5x (avx512-2x16), Zen 4 2.1x (shani-x4), Zen 3 2.1x, Intel Emerald / Granite Rapids 2.0-2.1x, Apple M-series 6.8x but only against the sha2 software path (sha2 0.10 uses software SHA-256 on aarch64 unless its asm feature is enabled); Zen 5 7.82 us/batch (8654 MB/s) vs sha2 27.71 us (2443 MB/s). Versus C implementations: 60% faster than Firedancer and 39% faster than the best isa-l_crypto result on Zen 5, about 8% faster than Firedancer on Zen 4, about 2.2x on Zen 3, but 2-12% slower than Firedancer on Intel Emerald Rapids / Granite Rapids in measured runs. Hash chains: 7.3 ns/link at 32 chains vs sha2 45.4 ns on Zen 5 (page says 6.0x); on Apple, against sha2 with its asm feature (27.7 ns), the best is 14.5 ns, about 1.9x (derived from page data). OpenSSL: benches/wasm/README.md says the native neon-sha2-x4 batch (about 16 us; BENCHMARKS.md lists 16.25 us) is 2.7x faster than node:crypto (OpenSSL), whose crypto.hash one-shot took 42.89 us/batch (1578 MB/s) on an M4 Max (unpinned, read as ratios).
corrections.caveats: The crates.io repository field (https://github.com/spool-labs/tape-sha256) returns 404; the code lives at https://github.com/spool-labs/sha256 (README names the crate tape-sha256; head commit 5e72f67 'minor cleanup' of 2026-08-11 matches the crate's .cargo_vcs_info.json), so repo_url should be overridden to that repository. First-party measurements by the author, and the main baseline is the Rust sha2 crate, not OpenSSL. On x86 sha2 0.10.9 uses SHA-NI by runtime detection, so those ratios are against a hardware-accelerated serial baseline; on Apple the 6.8x batch figure is against the sha2 software path (the crate's asm feature, available here only as the sha2-asm-bench bench feature, was off), so the hardware-to-hardware Apple gain is much smaller (hash chains: 14.5 vs 27.7 ns, about 1.9x). The only OpenSSL comparison is through Node.js (per-call JS overhead included, M4 Max unpinned, native batch number from a different document than the node:crypto number, so cross-run). Same-machine paired runs, but rustc version, RUSTFLAGS and the Zen 5 and Apple CPU models are not captured; -C target-cpu=native made the Zen 5 kernel 8-14% slower. Does not win everywhere: 2-12% slower than Firedancer on Intel Emerald / Granite Rapids; the Firedancer harness builds prefix||leaf outside the timed region while tape reads prefix and body from separate slices. Results are single-core batch hashing, not application speedups (the README also cites 14-21% faster Agave shred recovery, unverified). Tests cross-check every backend against the sha2 crate. Very young project (first commit 2026-07-26), 1 GitHub star.
